Your own bot team. Built to cost less.
One keyboard. More places to put it to work.

Xavier

Think about the work you repeat every week: drafting a customer reply, turning a pile of notes into a clear brief, or finding the next step in a project. The BotBar idea is to put a team of useful bots where you already work, at the keyboard. You should be able to give each bot a purpose, then bring it into a supported workflow without starting over every time you change tasks. One bot might organize research. Another might turn that research into a draft. The value is the time between those steps that you get back.

The proposed model keeps local bots inexpensive to create and run, with paid cloud resources when the job needs more capacity. That gives someone a way to start small, tune a useful helper, and expand when the work justifies it. Local operation still uses your device and electricity, and connected services can have their own charges. We have not announced a firm monthly price or a team plan. The promise we are building toward is choice: the right amount of computing for the job, rather than an expensive model doing every tiny task.

Theo

Picture a small team that has different jobs but shares a common place to work. A business owner could have one bot preparing tomorrow’s content, another organizing incoming requests, and another keeping a project brief current. Those are examples of the intended experience, not a claim that every workflow is already available. You decide what each bot can do. Device reach depends on the supported runtime and integrations, so we should demonstrate the actual phone or computer setup rather than promise that every keyboard works today.

The exciting part is that a useful bot does not have to be a whole new app you commission from scratch. It can be a focused helper for a specific job. As the system develops, the goal is to make that helper available where it is useful, with local and cloud options that suit the work.

Johnny describes the ambition as the power of corporations in your pocket: focused helpers for research, email preparation and customer-service work that a small team would otherwise struggle to organize. That is the idea we want people to feel. The useful measure is the work they can actually get done, not the size of the slogan.

Qa

Pricing: Local bots are proposed as free to build/run at the platform level; device, provider and cloud costs can still apply. No finalized monthly price, supported-device matrix or per-user limit is established by these materials. Do not promise unlimited simultaneous execution.

Mostly built. Unmistakably yours.
Your know-how becomes the secret sauce.

Xavier

Most people do not want to become AI engineers. They want a result. BotBar’s approach is to start with useful components and let you shape the purpose, instructions and workflow. Your expertise becomes the part that makes the bot valuable: how you qualify a lead, how you explain your service, how you organize a brief, or how you review a finished piece of work. You should spend your effort teaching the bot what good looks like, rather than rebuilding basic plumbing.

Here is the practical difference Johnny is aiming for. Today, automating a simple task can turn into a maze of accounts, integrations and API setup. A keyboard and browser connection can offer another route for supported tasks: help you work through the interface you already use. If you are drafting a Facebook post, for example, the bot could help prepare the copy and work in the authorized browser workflow. That does not mean a keyboard automatically grants access to every account, bypasses login, or removes the service’s rules. Permissions and any required confirmation still matter. The point is less setup where the supported connection allows it.

Reusable open-source components can shorten the path when their licenses, quality and dependencies fit the job. The customization is where your knowledge matters. We are not attaching an unverified percentage to how much arrives prebuilt, or claiming a partnership because a component comes from a familiar institution.

Theo

The user experience should feel like tuning a helper. Tell it who it helps, what it does, and how you want the result. Give it your examples. Review a preview. Improve it as you learn what you need. A real estate professional and a care-service coordinator might start with some of the same underlying pieces but give their bots very different instructions and boundaries.

Imagine you are already writing a message and want a supporting document summarized. The goal is to ask from the place you are working and get a useful result back without losing your place. Then you can check it before sending anything. That is the pain BotBar is trying to remove: the repeated setup and context switching between an idea and a completed task. We should show one clear example all the way through, so the audience sees the difference instead of only hearing that it is easy.

Mostly built refers to the intended reusable-component experience, not a guarantee every requested bot is instantly deployable.

Bots with a job beyond the chat.
Your team can work with other trusted teams.

Xavier

A conversation can help you think. A connected bot can also carry a defined job forward when it has the right tools, runtime and permission. That is the distinction behind Johnny’s phrase about bots being confined to one place. BotBar aims to let your own bots operate across supported workflows and coordinate with other authorized bots. They can share the task context that you allow, hand over a result, and return something you can review.

Kloudy’s MCP connection is part of the coordination approach. In plain language, it provides a structured way for compatible agents to discover and call tools. It does not by itself prove that every bot is trusted or that every handoff will succeed. The system also needs clear ownership, access controls and reliable delivery. Our recent audio review is a good reminder that a conversation on a shared line and dependable tool coordination are different things. We should demonstrate both honestly.

The long-term value is a workflow that can keep moving while you focus elsewhere. A permitted overnight job could organize research and prepare a morning brief. It needs an available runtime, spending limits and an explicit scope. It should pause or ask rather than turn an unclear instruction into an unwanted commitment.

Theo

Think of your bot as a representative of the way you work. During the day you guide it. With the right setup, it can keep preparing approved work while you sleep, or collaborate with a friend’s bot when both owners have allowed that exchange. One bot could gather permitted material and another could turn it into a draft. You would return to a result and a record of what happened.

Grok, Muse and Dots can be part of the broader experience through supported connections, but your custom bots can have their own focused jobs and settings. We should not claim that other providers have approved every integration or that their assistants automatically arrive with every installation. The opportunity is to make a team of different capabilities useful together, while the person stays in charge of what crosses between them.

Persistence means keeping the job and its context available beyond one chat session. In a supported browser or email workflow, an authorized bot could prepare a reply or collect information, and another could help check it. Customer-service automation needs a defined scope, escalation to a person and a reliable record. Those are the design responsibilities that make the vision useful.

$9.5B in AI app-development platforms
Gartner’s 2026 forecast

Xavier

The market context is substantial, but we should use a category we can name clearly. Gartner forecasts worldwide AI application development platform spending at 9.541 billion dollars in 2026. That is a relevant reference point for a platform that helps people create and use bots. It is not proof that the entire category is available to BotBar, and it does not tell us what this company will earn.

For scale, one percent of that forecast is 95.41 million dollars in annual category spending. That is an illustration of the size of a small share, not a revenue forecast, valuation or promise of investment returns. Reaching even a fraction requires a clear customer, reliable product, distribution and retention. The useful investor question is: which people will use this every week, what will they pay for, and can we serve them profitably?

The funding purpose Johnny described is concrete: make the platform easier for people to use, improve dependable delivery, and provide the customer service required to support adoption. We have not supplied a raise amount, valuation or investment terms. The ask should connect resources to measurable product milestones, rather than treating a large industry number as a business plan.

Theo

The strongest story is that the opportunity comes from useful work repeated by real customers. Start with a workflow someone needs, make setup easier, and make the result reliable enough that they come back. Then show how that expands to a team or another workflow. That is a more persuasive path to growth than simply saying AI is a large market.

Capital can help turn a working idea into a service people can depend on: clearer onboarding, stronger testing across the supported devices, practical support when a customer gets stuck, and measured operating costs. Those are proposed priorities for the funding, not an allocation or budget already approved. A future investment discussion needs the actual plan, terms and evidence. Today, the point is the scale of the category and the specific work required to earn a place in it.

Whoever controls the keyboard
controls the screen.

Xavier

The keyboard is a strategic place because it sits at the point where people turn an intention into an action. They write a message, direct a search, begin a document or ask for help. BotBar’s vision is to make that familiar place intelligent, so the next useful bot or action can be close at hand instead of hidden in a separate app. The person still controls the device. The phrase about controlling the screen is a positioning idea, not a claim that BotBar owns every app or bypasses the operating system.

That position could also support a commercial model beyond cloud usage. A relevant, clearly labeled offer could appear in a supported BotBar surface when the person wants it. Think of a useful product or service near the moment it is needed, not an advertisement interrupting everything the user types. That is an advertising vision, not a confirmed ad network, reach figure or revenue stream. Privacy and user choice have to be part of the design.

The close is simple: give people a useful team where their work begins. If that team consistently saves time, the keyboard becomes a place they choose to return to. That is the foundation the wider business has to earn.

Theo

Johnny’s table metaphor brings the whole idea together. The keyboard is the table, your bots are the teammates, and the work is yours. You can bring your expertise, choose a helper, and decide what should happen next. The goal is continuity across supported apps and devices, rather than starting the relationship again every time you move.

There is an attractive distribution idea here: a useful surface that people meet during their normal work. But its reach depends on what is supported and what the person enables. We should not say it is always visible through every app, browser or phone today. The vision is a familiar place that can travel with your workflow, with relevant services and bots available when you want them. The final invitation is to look at the real demonstration, name the work you want help with, and see whether the experience makes that work easier.
